### TweenOptions

*interface*

A tween's timing and callbacks (since API\_MINOR 37). Times are seconds of the frames' deltas.

```ts
export interface TweenOptions { … }
```

- `duration?: number;`

  Seconds a run takes (default 1; 0 jumps to the end values).

- `delay?: number;`

  Seconds before it starts (default 0).

- `easing?: EasingName;`

  Default `"linear"`.

- `repeat?: number;`

  Runs after the first (default 0; `Infinity` repeats until stopped).

- `yoyo?: boolean;`

  Every other run goes back from the end values to the start values with the same easing (tween.js's yoyo).

- `repeatDelay?: number;`

  Seconds before each repeat, held at the run's end (default 0).

- `from?: Record<string, unknown>;`

  Start values for some of the tweened properties, in the same forms as `to` (default: each property's value when the tween starts).

- `paused?: boolean;`

  Starts paused.

- `onComplete?: () => void;`

  Once it finishes (not when stopped), after its end values were written.

- `onRepeat?: () => void;`

  As each repeat begins.

### tween

*function*

```ts
export function tween(target: object, to: Record<string, unknown>, options?: TweenOptions): Tween;
```

Since API\_MINOR 37 (`TWEENS_MINOR`; older games' calls throw a TypeError): eases `target`'s properties to the values in `to`, stepped by the runtime itself, so no script runs a frame for a tween's timing and easing. A property is

- a number (`material.opacity`, `light.intensity`, a uniform's `value`, any numeric field of a plain object);
- a Vector2, Vector3 or Vector4 (`position`, `scale`): `to` gives a vector, `{ x, y, z }`, `[x, y, z]` or one number for every component;
- a Color (`material.color`, `emissive`): any `ColorLike`, lerped in linear light as `Color.lerp`;
- an Euler (`rotation`): `[x, y, z]` or `{ x, y, z }`, its angles lerped and set with `rotation.set` (its order kept);
- a Quaternion (`quaternion`): a quaternion, `[x, y, z, w]` or an Euler, slerped as three.js r185's `Quaternion.slerp` and set with `quaternion.set`.

So `tween(mesh, { position: [0, 2, 0], scale: 1.5 })`, `tween(mesh.material, { opacity: 0 })` and `tween(material.uniforms.glow, { value: 1 })`.

Timing is tween.js's (three.js's examples' tween library) in seconds: after `delay`, `repeat + 1` runs of `duration`, each repeat after `repeatDelay`; the start values are read as the tween starts (as its delay ends) unless `from` gives them. Once a frame, just before `onUpdate` (and `nextFrame`'s callbacks), every running tween advances by the frame's delta (`frame().delta`) and its values are written as plain assignments (`position.x = …`; Euler and Quaternion through their `set`, so the other follows), so script reads them as it would its own and `onUpdate` may still change them. Then, in the order the tweens were made, repeats call `onRepeat` and finished tweens call `onComplete` and resolve `finished`. Time is summed from the frames' deltas and the easings use the engine's own powers and angles, so the same frames give the same values bit for bit natively and in browsers (replays and render checks repeat).

A tween takes over the properties it drives as it starts: an older tween of the same property of the same object lets that property go, and stops (`finished` false) once it drives none. A property a plain assignment cannot store (read-only, a getter without a setter, a frozen or non-extensible object's, an array's `length`) throws a TypeError here. At most 16,384 tweens at once (RangeError) and 64 properties a tween; a step costs the frame's fuel about one unit a tweened property.

### Tween

*class*

A running tween (since API\_MINOR 37), made by `tween`.

```ts
export class Tween { … }
```

- `private constructor();`

- `readonly target: object;`

  The object `tween` was given.

- `readonly finished: Promise<boolean>;`

  Resolves true when it finishes, false when it is stopped (`stop`, `stopTweens`, or other tweens took all its properties over).

- `readonly running: boolean;`

  Whether it is waiting out its delay or running.

- `paused: boolean;`

  A paused tween keeps its values and its place in time.

- `pause(): this;`
- `resume(): this;`

- `readonly progress: number;`

  Its current run's progress before easing, 0 to 1 (0 while delayed, 1 once it ended).

- `stop(): this;`

  Stops it where it is: `finished` resolves false, no `onComplete`.

- `end(): this;`

  Writes the values its last run ends on (for a tween repeating forever, the end of a forward run) and finishes it at once: `onComplete` runs and `finished` resolves true.

### ease

*function*

```ts
export function ease(name: EasingName, t: number): number;
```

Since API\_MINOR 37: easing `name` at `t` (0 to 1 is the run; the curves go on outside it), the values tweens use.

### stopTweens

*function*

```ts
export function stopTweens(target?: object): void;
```

Since API\_MINOR 37: stops the tweens `tween` was given `target` for, or every tween without one.

### Line

*class*

A line through the geometry's `position` vertices (three.js `Line`, since API\_MINOR 17), by its index when it has one, within its draw range, drawn one pixel wide with a `LineBasicMaterial` (another material is a TypeError as the scene syncs). Lines cast no shadows, take no part in ambient occlusion or the scene-depth texture (`renderer.sceneDepth`), are culled by their vertices' bounds, and rays pass through them (three.js's line picking and `raycaster.params.Line` are not supported). A geometry a line draws makes a line mesh, counted against the mesh budget, which lines drawing that geometry alike (the same kind, with or without its colors) share; changing its positions, colors, index or draw range makes it again.

```ts

```

- `readonly isLine: true;`
- `geometry: BufferGeometry;`
- `material: LineBasicMaterial;`

## Cameras

### Camera

*class*

Objects and lights parented to a camera (a held item, a headlamp) draw only once the camera itself is added to the scene, as in three.js.

```ts
export abstract class Camera extends Object3D { … }
```

- `near: number;`
- `far: number;`

- `projectionMatrix: Matrix4;`

  As three.js: from the camera's own aspect or edges. Before API\_MINOR 20 the window's camera (`renderer.camera`) without a view offset takes the window's current aspect, as it draws; every other camera (one kept for maths, such as a probe a view is fitted through, for `project`, `unproject`, `Raycaster.setFromCamera` or a `Frustum`) takes its own on every minor.

  Since API\_MINOR 34 (`CAMERA_PROJECTION_MINOR`) it is the camera's own Matrix4, as three.js's: a game may write its elements (or assign another Matrix4), and the camera then draws with what it holds until `updateProjectionMatrix()` makes it again from the camera's settings. That is three.js's Reflector's oblique near plane (elements 2, 6, 10 and 14 from the mirror plane, so the mirror camera clips exactly at it), or any projection a port builds (`makePerspective`, a jittered or shifted frustum). A written matrix decides the frame's clipping, depth and frustum culling (from its own clip volume, so an oblique near plane culls what lies wholly beyond it), `project`, `unproject` and `Raycaster.setFromCamera`, the background's directions, and the post effects' and ambient occlusion's projection; `near` and `far` stay the camera's (picking rays start at `near`, shadow cascades slice `near` to `far`, and `sceneDepth` and fog measure distance along the view axis, so neither reads the projection). The matrix is three.js's WebGL one (clip depth -1 to 1), mapped to each GPU's own. Unlike three.js, a camera whose matrix was never written follows its settings at once (changing `fov` draws without `updateProjectionMatrix()`, as on older minors). A matrix that is not finite draws with the settings' projection; a singular one draws nothing. Before API\_MINOR 34 it is read-only in effect: it is made from the settings each time it is read, and what a game writes into it is lost.

- `projectionMatrixInverse: Matrix4;`

  The projection's inverse. Since API\_MINOR 34 a game may write it as three.js's Reflector does (`projectionMatrixInverse.copy( projectionMatrix).invert()`); unless written it is the inverse of `projectionMatrix` as it is then (written or made).

- `readonly matrixWorldInverse: Matrix4;`

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

  three.js's: since API\_MINOR 34 it makes `projectionMatrix` (and its inverse) from the camera's settings again, dropping a written one; before it the projection follows the settings without it.

### CameraView

*interface*

A camera's view offset (three.js `camera.view`, since API\_MINOR 16): what `setViewOffset` sets. Its fields may be changed in place, as in three.js; the scene's sync reads them.

```ts
export interface CameraView { … }
```

- `enabled: boolean;`
- `fullWidth: number;`
- `fullHeight: number;`
- `offsetX: number;`
- `offsetY: number;`
- `width: number;`
- `height: number;`

### PerspectiveCamera

*class*

Looks down its -Z. `fov` is the vertical field of view in degrees (three.js). From API\_MINOR 20 the projection takes `aspect` as three.js does (a game keeps it at the window's, `engine.frame()`'s width over height, or the image stretches); before it the aspect follows the window. `far` may be Infinity.

```ts
export class PerspectiveCamera extends Camera { … }
```

- `constructor(fov?: number, aspect?: number, near?: number, far?: number);`
- `fov: number;`

- `aspect: number;`

  From API\_MINOR 20 always the projection's, as three.js's. Before it the window's camera (`renderer.camera`) draws with the window's aspect without a view offset, and its `projectionMatrix` follows; with one, or for any other camera's `projectionMatrix`, it is used as three.js uses it (`setViewOffset` sets it to `fullWidth / fullHeight`).

- `view: CameraView | null;`

  three.js's view offset (since API\_MINOR 16): null until `setViewOffset`; `enabled` false after `clearViewOffset`.

- `setViewOffset(fullWidth: number, fullHeight: number, x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): void;`

  three.js `setViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): the window shows the `width` × `height` part at `x`, `y` (from the top-left corner, y down) of a `fullWidth` × `fullHeight` image the camera would fill, in any units, and `aspect` becomes `fullWidth / fullHeight`. The projection is then three.js's own, which moves its centre: say, `setViewOffset(w, h, -panel, 0, w + panel, h)` keeps what the camera looks at centred in the window's right `w` beside a `panel` on the left. A size of 0 or a value that is not finite draws nothing, as in three.js. Natively and in browsers alike.

- `clearViewOffset(): void;`

  three.js `clearViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): the projection is centered on the window's aspect again.

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

  Kept for ports; projection changes apply without it (since API\_MINOR 34 it also drops a written `projectionMatrix`, as in three.js).

### OrthographicCamera

*class*

From API\_MINOR 20 three.js's projection: `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` (asymmetric ones too) and `zoom` as given, whatever the window's aspect (a game keeps `right - left` at the window's aspect times `top - bottom`, or the image stretches, as in three.js; nothing changes them when the window does). Before it the view is centered: `top - bottom` sets its height in world units and the width follows the window's aspect (`left`/`right` are kept but not used for the extent, unless a view offset is set); that is the window's camera's (`renderer.camera`) drawing and `projectionMatrix`, while any other camera's `projectionMatrix` is three.js's on every minor.

```ts
export class OrthographicCamera extends Camera { … }
```

- `constructor(left?: number, right?: number, top?: number, bottom?: number, near?: number, far?: number);`
- `left: number;`
- `right: number;`
- `top: number;`
- `bottom: number;`
- `zoom: number;`

- `view: CameraView | null;`

  three.js's view offset (since API\_MINOR 16), as `PerspectiveCamera.view`.

- `setViewOffset(fullWidth: number, fullHeight: number, x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): void;`

  three.js `setViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): while it is set the projection is three.js's from `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` and `zoom` (so `right - left` should keep the window's aspect), showing the `width` × `height` part at `x`, `y` of the `fullWidth` × `fullHeight` image they span.

- `clearViewOffset(): void;`

  three.js `clearViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16).

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

## Lights

Intensities (top of file) are three.js r155+'s from API\_MINOR 23, so a port keeps three.js's; before it they are the engine's legacy ones, π times those, and a port from r155+ divides every light's `intensity` here by `Math.PI`. At most 16 lights besides ambient light draw, and four shadow-casting lights: the first four directional or spot lights (in scene order) with `castShadow` cast, each with its own shadow map; other lights' shadows are ignored.

### Light

*class*

```ts
export abstract class Light extends Object3D { … }
```

- `color: Color;`
- `intensity: number;`

### AmbientLight

*class*

Adds color × intensity of irradiance to every lit surface (ambient lights add up): from API\_MINOR 23 through three.js's `BRDF_Lambert`, `base × (1 − metalness) / π` of it, as three.js r155+; before, the legacy units' color × intensity × the whole base color.

```ts
export class AmbientLight extends Light { … }
```

- `constructor(color?: ColorInput, intensity?: number);`

### LightShadow

*interface*

Shadow settings of a casting light.

Since API\_MINOR 23 (games declaring `engine.minor=23` or later) they are three.js r185's `LightShadow`: the map sees what `camera` sees from the light's world position looking at its target's (up +Y), as three.js's `updateMatrices`. A directional light's camera is an `OrthographicCamera(-5, 5, 5, -5, 0.5, 500)`: shadows reach only what its box holds (outside it all is lit), and the box's width over `mapSize` is a texel's size, so the bias a scene needs is the one it needs in three.js. A spot's is a `PerspectiveCamera` whose `fov` is twice the light's `angle` times `focus` (degrees), its aspect `aspect` and its far plane the light's `distance` (or the camera's own `far`, default 500, without one), near 0.5. Set the camera's planes, edges and `zoom` and call its `updateProjectionMatrix()` as in three.js; the shadow follows them each frame. Shadows filter as `renderer.shadowMap.type` says (`PCFShadowMap`: five lookups on a Vogel disk `radius` texels wide, turned per pixel by interleaved gradient noise; `BasicShadowMap`: one nearest texel). Maps draw each material's `shadowSide` (by default the side opposite its `side`), clipped at the camera's near and far planes, a masked material cut out by its map's alpha alone (`alphaTest` against `map`, as three.js's `MeshDepthMaterial`; not `opacity` or vertex colors).

Before API\_MINOR 23 they are the engine's own: a directional light's map is fitted to the camera's view out to `distance`, `bias` acts only when negative and `normalBias` is in map texels (the members marked "before API\_MINOR 23"); the camera's `near` and `far` are `near` and `distance`, and three.js's members below are ignored.

Since API\_MINOR 33 a light may take the engine's receiver-plane filter in place of three.js's (`receiverPlane`, not three.js).

Before API\_MINOR 40 point lights cast no shadows. Since API\_MINOR 40 a point light's `shadow` is three.js r185's `PointLightShadow` (see `PointLight.shadow`). At most four maps are drawn: the directional and spot lights' with `castShadow` in scene order (each cascade a map), then point lights', so point lights lose theirs first, to the slots and to the effect budget (with a note in Options).

```ts
export interface LightShadow { … }
```

- `camera: OrthographicCamera | PerspectiveCamera;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 the shadow camera (an `OrthographicCamera`, or a spot's `PerspectiveCamera`), which three.js's `copy` clones.

- `mapSize: Vector2 | number;`

  The map's size, 64–4096: a three.js vector (its larger side when not square) or a number. Since API\_MINOR 23 the default is 512 × 512 and the game's size is kept whatever the graphics level (sizes past 4096, or past the device's largest texture, draw at the smaller; each map takes size² × 4 bytes of the GPU's effect budget, and one that does not fit is left out, its light unshadowed, with a note in Options). Before it the default is 2048, and since API\_MINOR 14 the graphics level holds it to its `shadowMapSize` (512 at quantum, 1024 atomic and molecular, 2048 cellular and terrestrial, 4096 above).

- `bias: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 added to the depth each point is compared at, in the map's 0–1 depth (default 0): negative values move it toward the light, against acne, positive ones away, as three.js's. Before it three.js's sign with only negative values acting (default −0.0005).

- `normalBias: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 how far each point moves along its vertex normal (turned for back-sided materials) before its lookup, in world units (default 0), as three.js's. Before it a normal offset in map texels (default 1.5).

- `radius: number;`

  The filter's radius in map texels, 0–16 (since API\_MINOR 9; three.js `shadow.radius`, default 1; 0 a hard edge): since API\_MINOR 23 the disk `PCFShadowMap`'s five lookups spread over, before it the spacing of the engine's nine. Outside 0–16 the light's sync throws.

- `intensity: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23: how much the shadow darkens, 0–1 (default 1).

- `focus: number;`

  Spot: the part of the cone the map covers, 0 &lt; focus ≤ 1 (three.js `shadow.focus`, default 1).

- `aspect: number;`

  Spot, since API\_MINOR 23: the camera's aspect (default 1).

- `blurSamples: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23, three.js's (default 8): `VSMShadowMap`'s blur, which the engine does not draw (VSM draws as PCF).

- `autoUpdate: boolean;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23, three.js's (default true and false). Since API\_MINOR 40 they act as three.js r185's: with `autoUpdate` false the map is drawn once and then kept, with the camera it was drawn with (the light may move; its map and lookup do not follow), until `needsUpdate` is set true, which draws it again that frame and goes back to false (`renderer.shadowMap.autoUpdate` and `needsUpdate` do the same for every map). Before API\_MINOR 40 the engine draws every map each frame whatever they say.

- `needsUpdate: boolean;`

- `distance: number;`

  Before API\_MINOR 23: a directional light's reach along the view (default 40 m), a spot's far plane.

- `near: number;`

  Before API\_MINOR 23: a spot's near plane (default 0.5 m).

- ```ts
  cascades?: {
      count?: number;
      maxDistance: number;
      splitLambda?: number;
      /** ENGINE EXTENSION (since API_MINOR 40, after Solstice's cached
       * shadows; default false): the cascades keep their static casters.
       * Casters that have not moved for 30 frames (and are neither skinned
       * nor drawn through a custom material's code) are drawn once into a
       * cache image per cascade, which is copied into the map each frame
       * with the casters that move drawn over it; a cascade draws its
       * cache again only when its view moves a coarse step (a 32nd of its
       * padded width, in whole texels) or out of its padded depth range,
       * when the light turns past its lag (0.03° for the nearest cascade
       * to 0.37° for the farthest), or when a caster joins or leaves the
       * cached ones (starts or
       * stops moving, appears or goes). Far cascades take turns: at most
       * one draws its cache again a frame. Each cache takes another map's
       * bytes of the effect budget; one that does not fit draws every
       * caster each frame, as without it. Not a boolean is a TypeError;
       * before API_MINOR 40 it is not read. */
      cached?: boolean;
    } | null;
  ```

  ENGINE EXTENSION, not three.js (since API\_MINOR 26; three.js's cascaded shadows are its `three/addons/csm` addon): a directional light's cascaded shadow maps, null (the default) for the one map of its `camera`'s box. With cascades the camera's box and planes are not used: `count` maps (1–4, default 3; each `mapSize`, together within the four maps a pass takes, so other casting lights may lose theirs) split the camera's view from its near plane to `maxDistance` (along the view; its far plane if nearer) as the CSM addon's practical split does, `splitLambda` (0–1, default 0.5, the addon's) blending its even split (0) with its logarithmic one (1). Each map is fitted to its slice, finest nearest, and a point takes the first map holding it. Past the last map (its square box covers the view to `maxDistance` and somewhat beyond, more so for wide views) the light is unshadowed, and casters out of a map's reach are not drawn into it: the cheap way to shadow a large world. `bias`, `normalBias`, `radius`, `intensity` and `renderer.shadowMap.type` apply to every map. Other values are a RangeError, and setting it before API\_MINOR 26 a TypeError, as the scene syncs; spot lights ignore it.

- `receiverPlane?: boolean;`

  ENGINE EXTENSION, not three.js (since API\_MINOR 33; three.js r185 has no receiver-plane bias): a directional or spot light's receiver-plane filter, false (the default) for the filter `renderer.shadowMap.type` gives (three.js's, which shadows a sloped surface at a near-zero `bias`). With true the map is filtered over nine lookups on a square grid `radius` texels apart (one at radius 0), each blending the four texels around it as a linear filter does but comparing each texel at the receiver's plane extended to that texel's centre (its slope from the screen derivatives of the world position), less half a texel's change of that plane on each axis; taps and texels past the map's edge are lit, as is all outside the shadow camera's volume. A sloped surface no longer shadows itself while a true occluder still shadows it fully, so `bias` need only cover depth precision and curvature. `bias`, `normalBias`, `intensity` and cascades apply as before; `renderer.shadowMap.type` does not. It costs 36 depth comparisons a lookup (4 at radius 0; three.js's PCF: five filtered). Other values are a TypeError, as is setting it true before API\_MINOR 33, as the scene syncs. See spec rendering-and-quality.html#receiver-plane.

### DirectionalLight

*class*

Light from `position` toward `target`'s position (three.js); both may be anywhere in the graph.

export class DirectionalLight extends Light { … }
```

### PointLight

*class*

`distance` is where its light ends (0: no limit); falls off with the distance to the power `decay` (2, the inverse square, as glTF).

```ts
export class PointLight extends Light { … }
```

- `constructor(color?: ColorInput, intensity?: number, distance?: number, decay?: number);`
- `distance: number;`
- `decay: number;`

- `readonly shadow: LightShadow;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40, three.js r185's `PointLightShadow` (undefined before): a `PerspectiveCamera(90, 1, 0.5, 500)` per cube face (its far the light's `distance` when set), `mapSize` each face's side (default 512; the map holds the six faces, 3 × `mapSize` square, so at most 1365 a face), `bias` in the face's 0–1 depth, `normalBias` in world units, `radius`, `intensity`, `autoUpdate` and `needsUpdate` as `LightShadow`'s; `PCFShadowMap` filters five lookups on a disk across the direction, `BasicShadowMap` compares the nearest texel, and points nearer than `near` or past `far` are lit, as three.js's `getPointShadow`. The engine has no cube textures: the six faces lie side by side in one 2D depth map.

### SpotLight

*class*

A cone toward `target`: `angle` (radians, at most π/2) is its edge and `penumbra` (0–1) the fraction of it that fades out. Point lights cast no shadows; spot lights can.

export class SpotLight extends Light { … }
```

- `angle: number;`
- `penumbra: number;`
- `decay: number;`
- `readonly shadow: LightShadow;`

*class*

Sky color from above blending to the ground color from below, by the surface normal, as irradiance: from API\_MINOR 23 through three.js's `BRDF_Lambert` of the diffuse color, `base × (1 − metalness) / π`, as three.js r155+; before, times the whole base color (legacy units).

### Scene

*class*

The scene the runtime draws (there is one: `scene`).

```ts
export class Scene extends Object3D { … }
```

- `#private;`
- `private constructor();`

- `background: Color | Texture | null;`

  What is behind everything (three.js), in the window and in `renderer.render(scene, camera)` passes into a render target (which once took only `renderer.setClearColor`): a Color clears to it (a pass of the scene clears to it whatever `autoClear` says, as three.js's does), never tone mapped; before API\_MINOR 20 the window's was tone mapped with the scene when post effects or multisampling drew it (from API\_MINOR 20 only when a `renderer.post` program reads the scene); null keeps black (a pass the renderer's clear color). Since API\_MINOR 18 a texture too, drawn over the clear behind everything, unfogged, tone mapped unless its `colorSpace` is `SRGBColorSpace` (three.js r16x's `WebGLBackground`):

  - a Texture or CanvasTexture of `UVMapping` (the default) stretched over the view, its UVs from the view's bottom left as a plane's through its `offset`, `repeat`, `rotation` and `center` (three.js leaves the aspect to them: `repeat.x = viewAspect / imageAspect` and `offset.x = (1 - repeat.x) / 2` cover a wider view);
  - a sky in every direction: a CubeTexture (its images at full detail: package paths load through `TextureLoader` once, counted against the image budget like any texture; nothing shows until all six have; one that cannot load shows the environment instead), a texture whose `mapping` is `EquirectangularReflectionMapping` (or `EquirectangularRefractionMapping`), or a PMREM texture (`PMREMGenerator`'s, which shows its prefiltered 512 × 256 image). `backgroundBlurriness` above 0 shows the sky's prefiltered environment at that roughness (made as `scene.environment` makes one, and shared with it for the same texture: it shows a few frames later); a `FloatType` DataTexture's light past 1 comes from it too. Other values draw nothing.

- `backgroundBlurriness: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: a sky background's blur, 0 (sharp, the default) to 1 (three.js `backgroundBlurriness`; clamped).

- `backgroundIntensity: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: a texture or sky background's light is its image's times this (three.js `backgroundIntensity`; default 1).

- `readonly backgroundRotation: Euler;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: turns a sky background (three.js `backgroundRotation`, as `environmentRotation` turns the environment).

- `fog: Fog | FogExp2 | null;`

- `environment: Texture | null;`

  Lights standard, physical and Lambert (since API\_MINOR 29 also Phong) materials without an `envMap` (three.js): a PMREM texture, a latitude-longitude texture or a CubeTexture (made into a prefiltered environment once per texture version; one that cannot be lights nothing, with a warning).

- `environmentIntensity: number;`

  Default 1.

- `readonly environmentRotation: Euler;`

  Turns the environment (three.js `environmentRotation`).

- `overrideMaterial: Material | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 35 (`OVERRIDE_MATERIAL_MINOR`; absent before): three.js r185's `overrideMaterial` (default null). While set, every pass of the scene (`renderer.render(scene, camera)` into a target, and the window's frame) draws each object with it in its own material's place: each keeps its geometry (and draw range, groups and morphs), placement, skin, instances, instance colors and shadow flags, and an object its own material hides stays hidden, as in three.js. A pass of an object under the scene ignores it, as three.js's does. Its kind decides what it takes: a `PointsMaterial` the points, a `LineBasicMaterial` the lines, a `wireframe` material the wireframes, any other material the triangle meshes (what an object draws is its own material's geometry here: one that draws lines, points or a wireframe keeps its own material under an override of another kind); sprites keep their own. Set it, render into a target, set it back to null: a depth or ID pass, a shadow map of the game's own.

### scene

*const*

```ts
export const scene: Scene;
```

### BloomSettings

*interface*

Bloom, three.js `UnrealBloomPass(resolution, strength, radius, threshold)` as it computes it: linear light whose luminance passes `threshold` is taken at half of `resolution` (the fraction of the frame the pass renders at, as a pass sized by its own `setSize`), blurred into five halved levels and added back, weighted by `strength` and `radius` (tight 0 to wide 1). Since API\_MINOR 29 it is three.js r185's: kernel radii 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22 with a sigma of a third of the radius, and the light added is 3 × strength times the weighted levels. Before, it is r176's (radii 3 to 11, sigma the radius, the sum added with additive blending by its alpha): 3 × strength² times the levels, so a game authored on three.js r176 or older keeps its bloom at 1.29 with about strength² as the strength; since API\_MINOR 30 `model` gives the older bloom exactly instead. Fields left out take the defaults.

```ts
export interface BloomSettings { … }
```

- `strength?: number;`

  0–65504, default 1 (`intensity`, accepted too, is its earlier name).

- `radius?: number;`

  0–1, default 0.

- `threshold?: number;`

  0–65504, default 0: above 1 only over-bright light (emissive surfaces driven past 1) blooms.

- `resolution?: number;`

  0.125–1, default 1.

- `intensity?: number;`

  @deprecated The strength's earlier name.

- `model?: "r185" | "r176" | "r160";`

  Since API\_MINOR 30 (a RangeError before): which three.js release's `UnrealBloomPass` to follow, default "r185". "r176" is the bloom of API\_MINOR 28 and older: kernel radii 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 with a sigma of the radius, normalized (nearly flat, so a small bright light spreads into a broad, squarish haze), the weighted sum added by its alpha (3 × strength² times the levels). "r160" is r176's with the high pass weighing light by Rec. 601 luma (0.299, 0.587, 0.114) where r176 and r185 take Rec. 709's. A port of a page on three.js r160 sets "r160" and keeps the page's strength as it is (not squared).

### AmbientOcclusionSettings

*interface*

Ground-truth ambient occlusion, three.js r176's `GTAOPass` with `OUTPUT.Default` (its `updateGtaoMaterial` and `updatePdMaterial` settings, `blendIntensity` and the fraction of the frame it renders at): the scene's meshes (not sprites, points or `noAO` objects) are drawn again as view-space normals and depth, front faces only; each pixel's occlusion comes from horizons searched within `radius` over `samples` steps, denoised, and multiplied into the light as `mix(1, occlusion, blendIntensity)` before bloom and tone mapping. Fields left out take three.js's defaults.

```ts
export interface AmbientOcclusionSettings { … }
```

- `blendIntensity?: number;`

  0–1, default 1.

- `radius?: number;`

  View units, above 0 up to 1000, default 0.25.

- `distanceExponent?: number;`

  0–16, default 1.

- `thickness?: number;`

  View units, 0–1000, default 1.

- `scale?: number;`

  The occlusion raised to this power, 0–16, default 1.

- `samples?: number;`

  Whole, 1–64, default 16.

- `distanceFallOff?: number;`

  0–1, default 1.

- `resolution?: number;`

  0.125–1, default 1.

- ```ts
  denoise?: {
      /** Above 0 up to 10000, default 10. */
      lumaPhi?: number;
      /** Above 0 up to 10000, default 2. */
      depthPhi?: number;
      /** 0–16, default 3. */
      normalPhi?: number;
      /** Pixels, 0–64, default 8. */
      radius?: number;
      /** 0–16, default 2. */
      rings?: number;
      /** Whole, 1–64, default 16. */
      samples?: number;
      /** 0–16, default 1. */
      radiusExponent?: number;
    };
  ```

  The Poisson denoise (`PoissonDenoiseShader`). three.js r176 keeps its disk's radius exponent at 1 until `updatePdMaterial` changes the samples, rings or exponent, and then uses 2 unless told otherwise: to match a call such as `updatePdMaterial({ samples: 8 })`, pass `radiusExponent: 2`.

### GradeSettings

*interface*

A color grade with a vignette. In `space` "linear" (the default) it comes after bloom and before the output's tone mapping (as a three.js `ShaderPass` before `OutputPass` sees the light), on linear light clamped to 0–1: an S-curve (`c²(3 − 2c)`) blended in by `contrast`, saturation around Rec. 601 luma, the result times `shadows`' tint turning into `highlights'` by a smoothstep of that luma from `split[0]` to `split[1]`, clamped, all blended with the ungraded light by `amount`; then light times `1 − vignette.amount × smoothstep(inner, outer, d)`, `d` the length of the offset from the frame's center in texture coordinates (0–1 across) with each axis times `vignette.scale`. Fields left out change nothing (the clamp aside). Since API\_MINOR 29 a linear grade also takes `levels` (the result times `levels[0]` plus `levels[1]` after the tints, a pass's `s = s * 0.98 + 0.015` lift) and `overRange: "keep"` (not clamped, and blended from the unclamped light with the light past 1 added back, `mix(c, s + max(c − 1, 0), amount)`, so over-bright light still reaches tone mapping), as games' grade passes often did; older games' grades ignore both. Since API\_MINOR 29 too, with any effect but multisampling on, a Color background is in the scene's light as three.js's `RenderPass` clears its composer target to it: occlusion, bloom, the grade, its vignette and the output take it too (from API\_MINOR 20 to 28 it shows as given, as a canvas without a composer).

In `space` "display" (since API\_MINOR 11) it works per channel on the tone-mapped, sRGB-encoded color `c` (clamped to 0–1), as a web page's canvas grade, in the same pass at no extra cost on every tier:

```text
l = 0.2126 c.r + 0.7152 c.g + 0.0722 c.b      (Rec. 709 luma)
k = night.brightScale > 0
    ? min(1, night.amount × night.brightScale) : 1
spare = max(smoothstep(night.warm[0], night.warm[1], c.r − c.b),
            smoothstep(night.bright[0], night.bright[1], l) × k)
n = night.amount × (1 − spare)
g = mix(l, c, saturation
              × (1 + night.spareSaturation × night.amount × spare)
              × (1 − night.desaturate × n))
g = (g − 0.5) × (1 + contrast) + 0.5
g ×= mix(shadows, highlights, smoothstep(split[0], split[1], l))
g ×= mix(1, night.tint, n)
g ×= 1 + lift.amount × smoothstep(lift.range[0], lift.range[1], l)
g = g × levels[0] + levels[1]    (since API_MINOR 30)
g += flash                       (flashSpace "display" only)
result = mix(c, clamp(g, 0, 1), amount) × the vignette's factor
```

(`mix(a, b, t) = a + (b − a)t`). Defaults leave each term out, so "display" with defaults is the plain saturation and contrast grade. The night desaturates before the split tints, so it does not grey them. With `contrastCurve` "s" (since API\_MINOR 30) the display grade starts from an S-curve instead of the slope, as ported pages' grade passes after `OutputPass` wrote it:

```text
s = mix(c, c²(3 − 2c), contrast)    (contrast 0–1)
l = 0.299 s.r + 0.587 s.g + 0.114 s.b    (Rec. 601 luma of s)
```

and everything above from `spare` on runs on s (in place of c) with this l and without the slope line; the result still blends from c. So royal-circuit's `vec3 s = mix(c, c * c * (3.0 - 2.0 * c), 0.22); float l = dot(s, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)); s = mix(vec3(l), s, 1.1); s *= mix(shadows, highlights, smoothstep(0.25, 0.85, l)); s = s * 0.98 + 0.015; c = mix(c, s, 1.0);` is `{ space: "display", contrastCurve: "s", contrast: 0.22, saturation: 1.1, split: [0.25, 0.85], shadows, highlights, levels: [0.98, 0.015] }` exactly (c and the result are within 0–1 on an 8-bit canvas, so the clamp changes nothing). With `luma` "709" (since API\_MINOR 31) the S-curve's l, in linear space or with `contrastCurve` "s", is Rec. 709 luma of s instead, `0.2126 s.r + 0.7152 s.g + 0.0722 s.b`, as pages such as city-fortune wrote theirs. `flash` is linear light added before tone mapping unless `flashSpace` is "display". Where post effects use 8-bit color the display grade still runs, without a linear flash (a display-space flash stays).

```ts
export interface GradeSettings { … }
```

- `space?: "linear" | "display";`

  Since API\_MINOR 11, default "linear".

- `contrast?: number;`

  Linear: the S-curve's weight, 0–1. Display: the slope about 0.5 less one, −1–3, or with `contrastCurve` "s" the S-curve's weight, 0–1. Default 0.

- `contrastCurve?: "linear" | "s";`

  Since API\_MINOR 30 (a RangeError before): the contrast's form. "linear" (display space only, its default) is the slope about 0.5 with Rec. 709 luma; "s" (linear space's only form, accepted there) blends in `c²(3 − 2c)` by `contrast` first and takes Rec. 601 luma of that curved color, as three.js grade passes do: it flattens near black where a slope crushes the darks.

- `luma?: "601" | "709";`

  Since API\_MINOR 31 (a RangeError before): the S-curved color's luma, which saturation and the split tints use. "601" (the default) is `0.299, 0.587, 0.114`; "709" is `0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722`, as some pages' grade passes take it: city-fortune's linear pass `float l = dot(s, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722));` is `luma: "709"`. Linear space, or display space with `contrastCurve` "s" only (the display slope has Rec. 709 luma already; a RangeError there).

- `keep?: { color: Color | number | string | readonly [number, number, number] | { r: number; g: number; b: number }; range?: [number, number] };`

  Since API\_MINOR 31 (a RangeError before): a key color the grade leaves alone, as a page's grade pass keeps its backdrop. Where the grade's input, clamped to 0..1 in the grade's space, lies within `range[0]` of `color` (Euclidean RGB distance) it is kept, ungraded and unvignetted, fading to the graded color by `range[1]` (default \[0.012, 0.05\], ascending within 0..2): `mix(graded, input, 1 - smoothstep(range[0], range[1], distance(input, color)))`. `color` is any Color form; a display grade compares it encoded (as `convertLinearToSRGB`), a linear grade as linear light, within 0..1. fourfold's `uKeep` pass is `{ space: "display", …, keep: { color: theme.bg } }` with the background cleared to the color ACES maps onto it.

- `saturation?: number;`

  0–4, default 1.

- `shadows?: readonly [number, number, number];`

  RGB multipliers (linear light, or encoded values in display space), each 0–4, default \[1, 1, 1\].

- `highlights?: readonly [number, number, number];`

- `split?: readonly [number, number];`

  Rising, each 0–1; default \[0, 1\] linear, \[0.2, 0.8\] display.

- `amount?: number;`

  0–1, default 1.

- ```ts
  vignette?: {
      /** 0–1, default 0. */
      amount?: number;
      /** 0–2 with `outer` beyond `inner`; defaults 0.5 and 1. */
      inner?: number;
      outer?: number;
      /** Each 0–4, default [1, 1]; [aspect ratio, 1] makes it round. */
      scale?: readonly [number, number];
    };
  ```

- `flash?: readonly [number, number, number];`

  Since API\_MINOR 9: linear light added to the whole frame before the grade and the tone mapping (a lightning flash), each 0–65504, default \[0, 0, 0\]. Like the grade, it needs the post effects' half floats (it is left out where they do not render).

- `flashSpace?: "linear" | "display";`

  Since API\_MINOR 11, display space only (a RangeError in linear space), default "linear": "display" adds `flash` to the graded display color after the night and the lift (so moonlight neither tints nor greys a lightning flash; values past 1 just reach white) instead of to the light before tone mapping.

- ```ts
  night?: {
      /** 0–1, default 0 (no night). */
      amount?: number;
      /** How far toward gray at full night, 0–1, default 1. */
      desaturate?: number;
      /** Moonlight multiplier, each 0–4, default [1, 1, 1]. */
      tint?: readonly [number, number, number];
      /** Red minus blue over which pixels are spared, rising, each −1–2;
       * default [1, 2] (none). */
      warm?: readonly [number, number];
      /** Luma over which pixels are spared, rising, each −1–2; default
       * [1, 2] (none). */
      bright?: readonly [number, number];
      /** Since API_MINOR 11: extra saturation of spared pixels at night
       * (fire and lamplight glow richer in the dark): their saturation
       * times `1 + spareSaturation × amount × spare`, 0–4, default 0. */
      spareSaturation?: number;
      /** Since API_MINOR 11: 0 (the default) spares bright pixels whatever
       * the night; above 0 (0–4) their spare is scaled by
       * `min(1, amount × brightScale)`, so near-white keeps its color only
       * as the night deepens (the warm spare is unchanged). */
      brightScale?: number;
    };
  ```

  Since API\_MINOR 11, display space only (a RangeError in linear space): a night look that desaturates and tints all but warm or bright pixels (fire, lamplight).

- `lift?: { amount?: number; range?: readonly [number, number] };`

  Since API\_MINOR 11, display space only: highlights times `1 + amount` (0–4, default 0) as luma rises through `range` (rising, each 0–1, default \[0.5, 1\]).

- `levels?: readonly [number, number];`

  The graded result's scale (0–4) and offset (−1–1), default \[1, 0\]: since API\_MINOR 29 in linear space, after the tints; since API\_MINOR 30 in display space too, on the encoded color after the tints and the lift, as a page's grade pass after `OutputPass` (such as `s = s * 0.98 + 0.015`) lifts it. A display grade's `levels` before API\_MINOR 30 is a RangeError.

- `overRange?: "clip" | "keep";`

  Since API\_MINOR 29, linear space only (display-space color is tone mapped and encoded, within 0–1, so there is nothing past 1 to keep: a RangeError there): "clip" (the default) clamps the light and the graded result to 0–1; "keep" grades the clamped light but adds the light past 1 back and blends from the unclamped light, as a pass writing `mix(c, s + max(c − 1, 0), amount)`.

### PostShader

*interface*

`renderer.post`'s program (since API\_MINOR 9), in the custom materials' WGSL and sandbox. `pixel` declares `fn pixel(p: Pixel) -> vec4f`, each pixel's linear light (its alpha the coverage: keep `scene_color(p.uv).a`), given

```text
struct Pixel { uv: vec2f, coord: vec4f }  uv 0..1 from the top left,
                                          coord the pixel's position
fn scene_color(uv: vec2f) -> vec4f   the scene's linear light
fn scene_depth(uv: vec2f) -> f32     view depth of the nearest
                                     opaque surface (65504: none)
fn world_position(uv: vec2f, depth: f32) -> vec3f
fn camera_position() -> vec3f, fn screen_size() -> vec2f
fn srgb_to_linear, fn linear_to_srgb
fn scene_velocity(uv: vec2f) -> vec3f  (since API_MINOR 40, an
                                     engine extension) the scene's
                                     motion: xy the offset in uv
                                     from this pixel to where its
                                     surface was the frame before
                                     (opaque and masked objects,
                                     their skins included; zero
                                     where nothing drew, the sky
                                     moving with the camera alone in
                                     the temporal resolve), z the
                                     reactive mask (coverage of
                                     transparent objects and
                                     particles). A program calling it
                                     brings the velocity pass along
                                     (the opaque objects' vertices
                                     again, plus 12 bytes a pixel of
                                     the scene). Custom materials'
                                     vertex hooks are not applied in
                                     it: their objects move as
                                     placed.
uniforms (numbers, vectors, matrices and vec4/matrix arrays; no
textures), 64 floats in whole vec4 slots; defines as constants.
```

export interface PostShader { … }

- `pixel: string;`
- `uniforms?: Record<string, ShaderUniform>;`

### AntialiasMode

*type*

```ts
export type AntialiasMode = "off" | "fxaa" | "smaa" | "msaa" | "taa";
```

Anti-aliasing: none, three.js's `FXAAShader` or `SMAAPass` (SMAA 1x) after the output, or 4× multisampling resolved before the other effects. Assigning `antialias` (any value, including "off") renders through the linear path: the scene in linear half-float color, fog and translucent or additive blending mixed in linear light before the output, so they look the same at every setting and the mode changes edges alone (since engine 1.36.2, at every API\_MINOR; "off" drew straight to the window before). A game that never sets it keeps three.js's canvas look: drawn straight to the window, fog and blending in encoded color. A device without half-float color draws an assigned "off" straight too (its 8-bit post buffers draw every mode that way).

"taa" (since API\_MINOR 40; a TypeError before) is the engine's temporal anti-aliasing with upscaling: the scene drawn with its projection jittered by a sub-pixel Halton(2, 3) offset over eight frames, each object's and skin's motion drawn into a velocity image, and every frame resolved with the last one's result reprojected by the nearest of its 3×3 pixels' motion, clipped to the neighbourhood's colours (no ghosting where something uncovers or changes), with less history under transparent objects and particles (the reactive mask), into the window's size: a scene at a render scale below 1 (`setPixelRatio`, `setSize`, the player's render scale and adaptive resolution) is upscaled by it. It runs before bloom and the output. three.js's `TAARenderPass` is different: it accumulates a still camera's jittered frames and starts again whenever anything moves. The history is dropped on a cut: a new `camera`, or `renderer.resetHistory()`. It needs half-float color and a depth format the device samples: without them FXAA stands in, with a note in Options.

### Renderer

*interface*

How the scene is drawn. The game decides the camera, lights, shadows on or off, fog, tone mapping, materials and the post effects, in three.js's `EffectComposer` order (since API\_MINOR 4; r185's passes since API\_MINOR 29, r176's before): the scene in linear half-float color (multisampled with `antialias: "msaa"`), `ao`, `bloom`, `grade`, the output (`toneMapping`, exposure, sRGB) and FXAA or SMAA; the player's graphics settings decide the shadow maps' largest size and multisampling's samples (since API\_MINOR 14, by the graphics level) and the frame rate, and a game usually picks its effects by `frame().quality` or `levelSettings()`. Light is linear and may exceed 1 (half-float range); `toneMapping` maps it to the display (none: clamped at 1). Effects that are off cost nothing; ones the device cannot run or that pass the GPU budget are left out with a note in Options (ambient occlusion first, then bloom, SMAA falling back to FXAA). Assigning a setting checks it: a TypeError for a value of the wrong type, a RangeError for one out of range (and the same, at the end of the frame, for an object changed afterwards).

```ts
export interface Renderer { … }
```

- `camera: Camera | null;`

  The camera the scene is seen through; nothing 3D draws without one. It need not be in the scene graph.

- `readonly shadowMap: { enabled: boolean; type: number; autoUpdate?: boolean; needsUpdate?: boolean };`

  `type` (since API\_MINOR 23): `PCFShadowMap` (the default) or `BasicShadowMap` (see `LightShadow`). `autoUpdate` and `needsUpdate` (since API\_MINOR 40, three.js r185's; true and false): with `autoUpdate` false no map is drawn, every one kept, until `needsUpdate` is set true for a frame.

- ```ts
  contactShadows?: {
      enabled?: boolean;
      light?: DirectionalLight;
      length?: number;
      thickness?: number;
      bias?: number;
      intensity?: number;
      steps?: number;
    } | null;
  ```

  ENGINE EXTENSION, not three.js (since API\_MINOR 40, after Solstice's deferred contact shadows; null, the default, for none): a short march from each pixel toward a directional light (`light`, or the first in the scene) through the scene's depth, `steps` (1–64, default 16) samples out to `length` world units (default 0.5): where a surface nearer the camera than a sample stands within `thickness` (default 0.1) past `bias` (default 0.01), the pixel's light is darkened by up to `intensity` (0–1, default 0.6), less the farther along. It draws as the post program over the scene, so it needs half-float color (otherwise it is left out with a note in Options), draws only while `renderer.post` is null, and darkens all of a pixel's light rather than the one light's: the small shadows where objects meet the ground that a shadow map's texels miss. Other values are a RangeError as the frame syncs.

- `bloom: BloomSettings | null;`

  Null (the default) for none.

- `ao: AmbientOcclusionSettings | null;`

  Null (the default) for none.

- `grade: GradeSettings | null;`

  Null (the default) for none.

- `post: PostShader | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 9: the game's own full-screen pass over the scene's light and depth (a thermal or night-vision view, height fog over everything, a screen-space curve), or null (the default). It runs after the scene is drawn and its ambient occlusion, before bloom, the grade and the tone mapping, on the post effects' half floats (setting it brings them along; where they do not render it is left out with a note in Options), in window frames (not render-target passes). The scene's depth is drawn first, as for `sceneDepth` (opaque objects only). Refused code is logged once and the scene draws without it.

- `antialias: AntialiasMode;`

  Default "off", never assigned: three.js's canvas look (see `AntialiasMode`; an assigned "off" draws as the other modes do, in linear light). "msaa" takes 4 samples; since API\_MINOR 14 the graphics level's `msaaSamples` (8 at cosmic and infinite, lowered to what the device supports) for games declaring `engine.minor=14` or later.

- `toneMapping: number;`

  three.js `toneMapping` (`NoToneMapping`, `LinearToneMapping`, `ReinhardToneMapping`, `CineonToneMapping`, `ACESFilmicToneMapping`, `AgXToneMapping`, `NeutralToneMapping`) with `toneMappingExposure` (default 1), applied to everything the scene draws.

- `toneMappingExposure: number;`

- `readonly capabilities: RendererCapabilities | undefined;`

  Since API\_MINOR 34 (three.js's `capabilities`, the members this engine has): whether `FloatType` render targets hold 32-bit floats on this device (`floatRenderable`; else half floats) and whether those filter linearly (`floatFilterable`; else they sample nearest). Undefined before API\_MINOR 34.

- `outputColorSpace: string;`

  three.js's output color space: `SRGBColorSpace` (the default) or, since API\_MINOR 26, `LinearSRGBColorSpace`, which writes the scene's light after tone mapping without the sRGB transfer (three.js r185's `linearToOutputTexel`): a `MeshBasicMaterial` of linear 0.25 (`setRGB(0.25, 0.25, 0.25)`, or `0x404040` with `ColorManagement.enabled` false) shows as `#404040` rather than `#898989`. The clear color, `scene.background` and fog colors are written in it too, and post effects' composite (bloom, grade) ends in it. Render-target passes are unchanged (linear light, as three.js), and so are the 2D draw layer and the UI, which are not the scene's output. Before API\_MINOR 26 the output is sRGB whatever this says.

Render targets (since API\_MINOR 8). The scene draws itself every frame; `render` draws into a render target.

- `setRenderTarget(target: RenderTarget | null, activeCubeFace?: number): void;`

  The target `render` and `clear` draw into, or null (the default); for a `WebGLArrayRenderTarget` (since API\_MINOR 34) the layer (three.js's `activeCubeFace`, default 0), for a `WebGL3DRenderTarget` (since 35) the slice.

- `getRenderTarget(): RenderTarget | null;`

- `autoClear: boolean;`

  Whether `render` clears the target to the clear color first (default true, as three.js). Set it false to draw over what the target holds: decals added over many frames, drawing only the new ones.

- `setViewport(x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): void;`

  The area of the render target `render` and `clear` draw into, from its bottom left, in its pixels (three.js); `setRenderTarget` sets it to the target's `viewport`. A pass into an area clears and draws only there (the area also scissors), the rest of the target kept: icons rendered into the cells of one atlas target. The camera's aspect is the game's (three.js's `camera.aspect`); a perspective camera here takes the area's. A RangeError at `render` for an area that does not lie within the target.

- `setViewport(viewport: Vector4): void;`
- `getViewport(target: Vector4): Vector4;`

- `setClearColor(color: ColorInput, alpha?: number): void;`

  The color (and alpha, default 1) targets clear to (default black).

- `getClearColor(target: Color): Color;`
- `setClearAlpha(alpha: number): void;`
- `getClearAlpha(): number;`

- `render(object?: Object3D, camera?: Camera): void;`

  Draws `object` and everything under it, as they are when it is called, through `camera` into the render target (three.js `render`): a `Group` kept out of the scene (an icon stage with its own lights, a batch of new decals) or the scene itself. Several calls in one frame draw in order, each with the objects as they were then (one stage gives many icons in a frame), before the frame's scene, so a material showing the target shows this frame's drawing. Materials are taken as they are at the call too, as three.js draws at once: color, opacity, blending and a custom material's `uniforms` values. One material stamped several times a frame with different uniforms between the calls draws each pass with that call's values (on every backend; since API\_MINOR 8). The window's scene, drawn at the frame's end, takes the values they have then. The object is placed by its parents, and only the lights under it light it; drawing the scene brings its fog, environment and background (a background color clears the area even without `autoClear`). Target passes draw without shadows and post effects (`bloom`, `ao`, `grade`, `antialias`), with `toneMapping`. A target's own texture cannot show in its pass (the pass is left out with a warning). Without a render target set, it does nothing (three.js ports calling it every frame keep working). A TypeError for an object that is not an Object3D, a camera that is not a Camera, or a disposed target; a RangeError past 256 passes a frame, or past 65,536 objects drawn by a frame's passes together.

- `clear(): void;`

  Clears the render target to the clear color (nothing without one).

- `readonly sceneDepth: Texture;`

  Since API\_MINOR 8: the scene's depth as a texture for custom materials (soft particles, shorelines): give it as a texture uniform and read red, the view depth (world units along the camera's forward axis) of the nearest opaque surface behind the fragment, at its window position: `textureSampleLevel(depth, depth_sampler, screen_uv(f.coord), 0.0).r`, compared with `view_depth(f.world)`. It holds the opaque objects (not blended, writing depth, not points, past alpha tests and vertex hooks) of the frame's scene, and 65504 where there are none. When a frame's objects sample it, the renderer first draws those opaque objects' depth (a prepass without shadows: their vertex work again, plus 12 bytes a pixel of the window); objects that sample it are not in it. Half floats keep about a two-thousandth of the distance. Render-target passes read the last frame's; where the device cannot render half floats it stays 65504. Nearest filtering by default (one object a game; disposing it does nothing).

- `readonly sceneColor: Texture | undefined;`

  Since API\_MINOR 34 (`SCENE_COLOR_MINOR`; undefined before): the scene's color as a texture for transparent custom materials (refraction, depth fog, shorelines; three.js's transmission pass): give it as a texture uniform and read it at the fragment's window position, offset for refraction: `textureSampleLevel(behind, behind_sampler, screen_uv(f.coord), 0.0)`. It holds the frame's background (sky, clear color) and the opaque objects drawn before the first blended object (or the first that samples it), in linear light (fogged, before the tone mapping and the output encoding; alpha the coverage), at the window's size, rows from the top. When a frame's objects sample it, the renderer copies the scene's color there (resolving it when multisampled) and draws the frame through the post effects' half floats, as `post` does, so that frame's blended objects blend in linear light (8 bytes a pixel of the window, plus the post buffers); frames whose objects do not sample it cost nothing. Objects that sample it, and blended objects before them, are not in it. Render-target passes read the last frame's; where the device cannot render half floats it stays transparent black. Linear filtering by default (one object a game; disposing it does nothing).

- `setPixelRatio(value: number): void;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (three.js's): the size the scene draws at is `setSize`'s width and height (logical pixels; the window's by default) times `setPixelRatio`'s ratio (the window's physical pixels per logical pixel by default), as a share of the window's width, within 0.25 to 2: a ratio of 1 on a 2× display draws the scene at half the window's size. The player's render scale and adaptive resolution (Options › Graphics) multiply it. The scene is then brought to the window's size: upscaled by `antialias: "taa"`, resampled linearly by the other modes (bringing the post effects' buffers along). Before API\_MINOR 40 `setPixelRatio` and `setSize` do nothing, the scene draws at the window's size and the getters, `setDrawingBufferSize` and `resetHistory` are undefined. A RangeError for a value that is not a positive finite number.

- `getPixelRatio(): number;`
- `setSize(width: number, height: number, updateStyle?: boolean): void;`
- `getSize(target: Vector2): Vector2;`

- `setDrawingBufferSize(width: number, height: number, pixelRatio: number): void;`

  `setSize(width, height)` and `setPixelRatio(pixelRatio)` at once.

- `getDrawingBufferSize(target: Vector2): Vector2;`

  `getSize` times `getPixelRatio`, rounded down.

- `readonly sceneVelocity: Texture;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (an engine extension; undefined before): the scene's motion as a texture for custom materials, as `sceneDepth` and `sceneColor` are: red and green the offset in uv from each pixel to where its surface was the frame before (previous minus current, rows from the top; zero where nothing opaque moved but the camera, whose motion the sky does not record), blue the reactive mask (transparent and particle coverage), alpha 1 where motion was drawn; at the scene's size, half floats, nearest filtering. Asking for it turns the motion vectors on (the opaque objects' vertices again, plus 12 bytes a pixel of the scene); window frames write it after the scene, so materials read the last frame's (a post program reads this frame's with `scene_velocity`). Zero where the device cannot render half floats.

- `resetHistory(): void;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40, an engine extension: drops the temporal history at the next frame (a cut to another shot or a teleport, so nothing of the last view is blended in; a new `camera` does it too).

- `ssr: SSRSettings | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): screen-space reflections, with three.js `SSRPass`'s settings, or null (the default). Each window frame traces, at half the scene's size, the view ray mirrored about each surface (its geometry normal, metalness and roughness factors, not its maps) through a min/max depth pyramid, takes the last frame's light where it hits (found through the motion vectors, which the effect turns on), accumulates it over frames and lays it over the scene before the post program, the temporal resolve and bloom. Misses (off screen, behind something, too far) keep the scene's own environment reflection. `opacity` (0..1, default 0.5), `maxDistance` (view units, default 180), `thickness` (how deep a surface is taken to be, view units, default 0.018), `distanceAttenuation` ((1 − distance / maxDistance)², default true) and `fresnel` ((1 + cos) / 2 of the incident and reflected rays, default true) are three.js's; `maxRoughness` (the roughest surface that reflects, 0..1, default 0.5; reflections fade out toward it) and `steps` (1..128, default 48) the engine's. Objects with `aoEnabled` false take no part (they neither reflect nor are reflected). It needs half-float color: off otherwise, noted in Options, and over the effect budget it goes after `ssgi`.

- `ssgi: SSGISettings | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): screen-space global illumination, or null (the default). The engine's (three.js's `SSGINode` names its settings): a probe at the centre of each 16 × 16 pixel tile traces sixteen rays over its hemisphere through the depth pyramid into the last frame's light, projected to L1 spherical harmonics, blended with like neighbours, interpolated per pixel along its normal, weighted by the ambient occlusion and accumulated over frames; the light found is added by each pixel's own color (an albedo the post buffers keep none of) less metalness. Misses keep the scene's own ambient and environment light. `giIntensity` (0..16, default 1), `radius` (how far rays reach, view units, default 5), `thickness` (view units, default 0.5), `stepCount` (1..128, default 24), `aoIntensity` (the ambient occlusion's share, 0..1, default 1) and `useTemporalFiltering` (default true). It runs at the High and Ultra quality tiers' levels only, needs half-float color (off otherwise, noted in Options) and is the first effect left out over the effect budget.

- `readonly exposure: { auto: AutoExposureSettings | null; hold: boolean };`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): exposure settings. `auto` (null by default) meters each frame's log luminance (weighted toward the centre) and brings its average to middle grey before tone mapping (with `toneMappingExposure` on top), easing toward it at `speed` (per second toward brighter, default 2) and `speedDown` (toward darker, default 0.46 × speed) within `minEv..maxEv` (EV100 of the average, −17..15, defaults −4 and 15), times 2^`compensation` (EV, default 0). With `night` (\{ minEv, maxEv \}) the limits move toward the night's as `daylight` falls (a number 0..1, or an object with a `daylight`, such as starhermit:sky's `SkyAtmosphere`, read each frame), so night stays dark. `hold` (default false) keeps the exposure as it is and leaves the frame unmetered, for a lightning flash. Where half floats do not render it meters and scales the tone-mapped image (within 1/8..8; noted in Options).

- `sharpen: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): contrast-adaptive sharpening of the shown image (0..1, default 0: none), after the output and any anti-aliasing, clamped to each pixel's neighbours so it leaves no halo.

- `film: { intensity?: number; grayscale?: boolean } | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): three.js `FilmPass`'s grain over the shown image (`intensity` 0..1, default 0.5; `grayscale` default false), or null (the default).

- `specularAntialiasing: boolean | { variance?: number; limit?: number };`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`SCREEN_EFFECTS_MINOR`; undefined before): specular anti-aliasing in the lit materials (default false, so their look stays three.js's): each pixel's squared roughness widened by the shading normal's variance across it (Toksvig, Kaplanyan et al.), so fine normal-mapped relief stops sparkling. `true`, or `{ variance, limit }` (the variance's scale 0..4, default 1; the most the squared roughness grows, 0..1, default 0.18). Reads back as a boolean.

- `capture(options?: { ui?: boolean }): Promise<Uint8Array>;`

  Since API\_MINOR 9: the frame this call makes, as the PNG bytes of a screenshot (a photo mode): the scene, and with `ui: true` the game's 2D overlay (`starhermit:draw`, `starhermit:ui`) over it, as drawn, opaque, at the window's drawable size. Never the runtime's own interface (Options, prompts, the not-responding screen, the on-screen touch controls), which is drawn after the capture is read: nothing the game could not draw. A frame larger than 3840 × 2160 is halved until it fits. The frame is read back as the runtime draws it and encoded off the drawing (natively on a thread, in browsers by the browser), so it settles a frame or more later and the game's frames go on meanwhile. Captures asked for in one frame all hold that frame (the same PNG for the same `ui`), and one asked for while earlier ones encode holds its own; at most 4 wait at once (a fifth rejects with `InvalidStateError`). One that could not be read, or was not encoded within 60 s, rejects with `EncodingError`: every capture settles. It needs no press; saving it does: `files.saveAs("photo.png", await renderer.capture(), { type: "image/png" })` in the press's handler. Since API\_MINOR 15 a capture asked for while uploads wait past a frame's upload bound (`engine.usage().waitingUploads`) holds the first frame that has sent every mesh and image made before it.

- `copyTextureToTexture?(srcTexture: Texture, dstTexture: Texture, srcRegion?: Box3 | null, dstPosition?: Vector3 | null, srcLevel?: number, dstLevel?: number): void;`

  Since API\_MINOR 35 (`VOLUME_TEXTURES_MINOR`; absent before): three.js r185's `copyTextureToTexture` for 3D textures, the engine's region update of one: the box `srcRegion` (a Box3 of whole texels, max exclusive; all of the source when null) of the Data3DTexture `srcTexture`'s `image.data` written into `dstTexture` (a Data3DTexture or a WebGL3DRenderTarget's texture, of the same format and type) at `dstPosition` (a Vector3; the origin when null), in order with the passes around it (`dstTexture`'s own pending data is sent first). Levels are 0. Other textures are a TypeError; a region outside either a RangeError.

- ```ts
  readRenderTargetPixelsAsync?(
      renderTarget: RenderTarget,
      x: number,
      y: number,
      width: number,
      height: number,
      buffer?: Uint8Array | Uint16Array | Float32Array,
      activeCubeFaceIndex?: number,
      textureIndex?: number,
    ): Promise<Uint8Array | Uint16Array | Float32Array>;
  ```

### Raycaster

*class*

Rays against meshes' triangles (sprites by their quads), nearest first. Only objects in the scene and visible are hit (as drawn: a raycast sends the frame's changes first). Tests at most 1,000,000 triangles a call (RangeError).

```ts
export class Raycaster { … }
```

- `constructor(origin?: Vector3, direction?: Vector3, near?: number, far?: number);`
- `near: number;`
- `far: number;`

- `readonly ray: Ray;`

  A Ray since API\_MINOR 18.

- `params: Record<string, Record<string, unknown>>;`

  three.js's per-kind settings, kept for ports (since API\_MINOR 17); not read: rays pass through lines and points.

- `layers: Layers;`

  The layers objects are tested on (since API\_MINOR 18): an object is hit when its `layers` share one with these (layer 0 by default). As three.js tests layers and not visibility, from API\_MINOR 18 (`engine.minor=18`) invisible objects, and objects under invisible parents, are hit when their layers match (ports pick with invisible proxy meshes; the ray's sync then sends invisible subtrees too). Games declaring an older minor keep invisible objects unhit. Only objects in the scene are hit, as before.

- `camera: Camera | null;`

  The camera of the last `setFromCamera` (since API\_MINOR 18).

- `set(origin: Vector3, direction: Vector3): void;`

- `setFromCamera(coords: Vector2, camera: Camera): void;`

  From normalized device coordinates (−1..1, y up) through a camera.

- `intersectObject(object: Object3D, recursive?: boolean, intersects?: Intersection[]): Intersection[];`

  Hits nearest first; since API\_MINOR 18 appended to `intersects` (sorted with what it held), as three.js.

- `intersectObjects(objects: readonly Object3D[], recursive?: boolean, intersects?: Intersection[]): Intersection[];`
